belief: I am a burden to everyone.
origins: Needing help with meals, driving, chores, or finances can make us feel like a weight on those we love. Guilt grows, and some people withdraw so as not to “bother” anyone. Often loved ones say they want to help, but the belief persists.
teaches: Paul writes, “Carry one another’s burdens, and in this way you will fulfill the law of Christ,” which assumes that all of us have burdens and all of us help carry them. Paul says “the parts of the body that seem to be weaker are indispensable” (1 Corinthians 12:22). Jesus welcomed those who needed help and said, “Come to Me, all you who are weary and burdened.” Receiving care is a gift that lets others love.
self_statements: They would be better off without me.
I am costing them too much.
I should not ask for help.
I am a weight on my family.
I wish I did not need anyone.
errors: Seeing myself as either independent or a burden.
Predicting that people will resent me.
Feeling guilty and concluding that I am a burden.
questions: What do my loved ones actually say about helping me?
What would I feel if I could help someone I love in this situation?
What do I still give to others?
What does Scripture say about weaker members?
How could I accept help in a way that lets others give?
Who could I speak with if the thought of being a burden becomes heavy?
truth: I am valuable to God and to the people who love me, not because of what I do for them. Receiving help is part of how love works, and my presence is a gift. If dark thoughts come, I will tell someone right away.
hw_truths: Receiving is a gift to others.
I am loved as I am.
log: Each week, note one time you received help gracefully.
actions: Tell them what you fear and listen to their answer.
Offer a prayer, a call, or a kind word.
If you ever feel life is not worth living, call or text 988 (U.S.) now.
prayer: Lord, I feel like a weight on those I love. Show me that I am valued, teach me to receive with grace, and let my life bless others in ways I cannot see. Amen.
